title: Why Montgomery Village Townhome Ducts Load Up Over Time
headline: Why Montgomery Village Townhome Ducts Load Up Over Time
description: Why Montgomery Village townhome ducts load up over time — 1970s runs, lake humidity, and tight dryer closets.

sections.heading: Fifty-year-old vent paths still serving modern appliances
paragraphs: When Kettler Brothers built Montgomery Village starting in the late 1960s, the standard residential dryer was a compact top-loader that exhausted through a short, straight vent. The furnace was a standing-pilot unit half the size of a modern air handler. Duct runs were calculated for that era's airflow needs. Today those same pathways carry output from high-capacity dryers and variable-speed blowers — equipment that pushes more air, more lint, and more moisture through passages that were never widened.

The mismatch is invisible from the living room. Inside the walls, lint accumulates at bends that were tight for 1972 and are tighter for 2024. Moisture that should exit the building in seconds lingers in the run, raising the humidity inside the mechanical closet and, by extension, the trunk lines inches away.

sections.heading: Lakeside micro-climate and what it means for lower-level trunks
paragraphs: Montgomery Village's lakes — South Valley Park, the Whetstone retention ponds, and the greenway channels through Stedwick — are shallow and warm from May through September. On calm evenings the water surface radiates moisture that collects in the lowest points of nearby neighborhoods. A townhome on Stedwick Road with a walkout lower level sits in that micro-climate pocket for hours each night.

The air handler in the lower level draws that humid air across a cold evaporator coil and pushes it into supply trunks that run through the ceiling above. Those trunks cool further as they extend toward upstairs registers. The temperature drop causes condensation, and any particulate matter already in the airstream — leaf fragments from the pathways, grass dust from the HOA's weekly mowing, general suburban pollen — adheres to the wet metal.

Dryer vents are a separate line from supply ducts — [NFPA research](https://www.nfpa.org/education-and-research/research/nfpa-research/fire-statistical-reports/home-fires-involving-clothes-dryers-and-washing-machines) ties many home dryer fires to failure to clean lint from the full run.

sections.heading: Weekly HOA maintenance creates a recurring pollen and debris cycle
paragraphs: The homeowner association maintains common areas on a strict schedule. Mowing crews cut paths and medians, blowing clippings and stirring pollen that settled overnight. Leaf-blowing in autumn sends a cloud of organic debris across parking areas and against townhome walls. All of this happens within feet of exterior return intakes and dryer exhaust caps.

A house with sealed windows and a clean filter handles a season reasonably well. Over several years, fine particles that pass a standard filter can deposit where airflow is slowest — bends and branch take-offs. Those deposits can grow enough that comfort or filter life changes; when debris is substantial or discharging into rooms, [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/should-you-have-air-ducts-your-home-cleaned) says cleaning is worth considering. We do not promise a fixed airflow percentage loss from any calendar interval.

sections.heading: Common signals in a Montgomery Village townhome
paragraphs: Because the housing stock is uniform, the warning signs tend to appear in a predictable order across the community:
listItems: A musty or stale smell from lower-level registers that strengthens during humid weeks and eases in winter.
A visible film — often greenish during spring, gray in autumn — on supply grilles in upstairs bedrooms.
Dryer cycles that stretch past the expected time, especially in summer when the vent run is already warm.

sections.heading: Resetting a system that has been accumulating for decades
paragraphs: A single cleaning appointment removes the accumulated film and debris that filters could not prevent. After that reset, the same filters work far more effectively because they are managing only new intake rather than recirculating embedded material. Running a dehumidifier in the lower level from late spring through early fall further slows the condensation cycle.
